description: A sequencer that runs Pascal's triangle: each clock builds the next cell of a row from the two cells before it, and three counters turn that cell into triggers and pitches.

params.text: Holding this down drives the clock high, which is what the clock input does with a gate in it.
Sets the cell the cursor is on to 1, which seeds a fresh pattern; holding it down keeps writing 1 every sample.
Stops the cursor moving on to the next row when it reaches the end of this one, so the same row is recomputed over and over.
Sets how many cells long a row is, 1 to 32; cells past that are cleared, so winding it down is a quick way to empty the grid.
Sets the modulus for that counter, 1 to 32: the counter fires whenever the current cell does not divide evenly by this, and the row itself is kept modulo the three moduli multiplied together.

inputs.text: A falling edge here computes the next cell of the row and moves the cursor on; the rising edge is what latches the pitch outputs.
A trigger here sets the cell the cursor is on to 1.
Above 1V the cursor stays on the current row instead of moving on to the next.
Adds to the length knob, 3.2 cells per volt, so 10V covers the whole 32.
Adds to that counter's modulus, 3.2 divisions per volt, so 10V covers the whole 32.

outputs.text: 10V for as long as the clock is high and the current cell does not divide evenly by that counter's modulus, 0V otherwise.
The current cell taken modulo that counter's modulus, one less, scaled so a full modulus would reach 10V; it is latched on the rising edge of the clock and held until the next cell that fires.
10V while the third counter is firing and its remainder is that number, so the six of them split the third counter's triggers across separate drums.

notes: Nothing moves without a clock: the grid is computed one cell per falling edge of the clock input or the clock button, and the module has no clock of its own.
The grid of lights is the triangle, four rows of 32 turned on their side, the cursor white; a cell takes red, green or blue for each counter whose modulus it does not divide by.
The row wraps round every four columns, so the fourth row is built from the first again.
The five blue lamps under each knob read that knob's setting as a binary number.
The grid and the lamps are lights rather than controls, so none of them can be clicked for help.
